meta_desc: Teach grade 4 money with decimals: rupees and paise in decimal form, adding bills and giving change. Free quiz and printable worksheet practice.
excerpt: Once a child sees that ₹45.75 is just 45 rupees and 75 paise wearing a decimal point, money maths clicks. Here is how I teach Grade 4 money with decimals, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 4 child a shop bill that reads ₹45.75 and ask what it means. Half will say ‘forty-five point seventy-five rupees’ and stop there. The ones who really understand grade 4 money with decimals will tell you it is 45 rupees and 75 paise — and that the little dot is the fence between the two. That single idea, that the decimal point separates rupees from paise, is the whole game at this level. Get it solid and the adding, subtracting and bill-solving fall into place.

In my experience teaching nine-year-olds, the trouble is almost never the arithmetic. It is that money looks like a different animal from the decimals in their maths book. It is not. One rupee is 100 paise, exactly the way one whole is 100 hundredths. So ₹0.05 is five paise, and ₹5.50 is five rupees and fifty paise, not five rupees and five paise. That last mix-up is the single most common error I see, so it is worth naming out loud.

Rupees and paise as a decimal

Start with the place-value picture, because it does the heavy lifting. In ₹45.75, the 4 is tens of rupees, the 5 is ones of rupees, the 7 is ten-paise, and the 5 is single paise. Read it as ‘forty-five rupees and seventy-five paise’, never ‘forty-five point seven five’ when money is involved. The naming keeps the meaning attached.

Two rules cover almost every conversion a Grade 4 child needs:

  • Paise to rupees: there are always two digits after the point. So 8 paise is ₹0.08, not ₹0.8. A stray missing zero turns eight paise into eighty.
  • Rupees-and-paise to decimal: write the rupees, a point, then the paise as a two-digit number. 12 rupees 5 paise becomes ₹12.05.

Adding and subtracting money with decimals

Here is the one habit that prevents most mistakes: line up the decimal points, one under the other, before you add or subtract. When the points are stacked, the rupees sit above rupees and the paise above paise automatically. Everything else is the column addition they already know.

Say a child buys a notebook for ₹28.50 and a pen for ₹12.75. Stack them so both points are in the same column, add the paise (50 + 75 = 125 paise, which is 1 rupee 25 paise, so carry the 1), then add the rupees. The total is ₹41.25. Subtraction for change works the same way — and if the paise column is too small, you borrow one rupee as 100 paise, exactly like borrowing a ten.

The zero trick for ‘short’ amounts

Children panic when the amounts have different lengths, like ₹9 minus ₹3.60. Teach them to write ₹9 as ₹9.00 first. Now both have two paise digits, the points line up, and 9.00 − 3.60 = ₹5.40 with no drama. Padding with zeros is not cheating; it is just writing the same amount more clearly.

Multiplying a price by a quantity

This is where money maths starts to feel useful. If one pencil costs ₹4.50 and you buy 6, you are doing 4.50 × 6. The shortcut I teach: ignore the point, multiply 450 × 6 = 2700, then put the point back two places from the right to get ₹27.00. Two paise digits go in, two come out. It works every time because you are really multiplying paise.

One honest caveat: do not rush to the shortcut. For the first week, let them add ₹4.50 six times so they feel why multiplication is faster. The trick without the reasoning tends to collapse under a slightly harder question.

Shopping, bills and change — the real test

Multi-step money problems are the point of all this. A typical one: Aarav has ₹100. He buys 2 chocolates at ₹18.50 each and one juice at ₹25. How much change does he get? Three steps, in order:

  • Cost of chocolates: 18.50 × 2 = ₹37.00.
  • Add the juice: 37.00 + 25.00 = ₹62.00.
  • Change from ₹100: 100.00 − 62.00 = ₹38.00.

The counter-intuitive bit for many children is that the answer is a whole number of rupees even though the prices had paise. That is a good thing to point out — it shows the paise cancelled out along the way, and it teaches them to sanity-check a total rather than trust the first number they write.

A weekly routine that works

Ten minutes a day, using real bills, beats a long Sunday session. Read a grocery receipt together and pick out the rupees and paise. Give ₹50 of pretend money and let them ‘buy’ two items and work out the change. Once a week, one written problem with three steps so they have to choose the order themselves. That choosing step is where fluency actually shows up.

Test what your child has learned

The short quiz below covers exactly this ground — converting rupees and paise, lining up the point to add, multiplying a price, and working out change. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.about: Grade 4 money written in decimal form (rupees and paise)

questions.q: How is 45 rupees 75 paise written in decimal form?
questions.explanation: The rupees go before the point and the paise (as two digits) go after: 45 rupees 75 paise is ₹45.75.

questions.q: What is 8 paise written in rupees?
questions.explanation: Paise always take two digits after the point, so 8 paise is ₹0.08. Writing ₹0.80 would mean 80 paise.

questions.q: Add ₹28.50 and ₹12.75. What is the total?
questions.explanation: Line up the points. 50 + 75 = 125 paise, which is 1 rupee 25 paise; carry the 1. 28 + 12 + 1 = 41, so the total is ₹41.25.

questions.q: A pencil costs ₹4.50. What do 6 pencils cost?
questions.explanation: 4.50 × 6: multiply 450 × 6 = 2700, then place the point two digits from the right to get ₹27.00.
Write ₹9 as ₹9.00 so the points line up, then 9.00 − 3.60 = ₹5.40.
305 paise is 3 rupees and 5 paise. Written as a decimal with two paise digits, that is ₹3.05.

questions.q: Riya buys items for ₹62.50 and pays with a ₹100 note. What change should she get?

faq.q: What does grade 4 money with decimals actually mean?
faq.a: It means writing money amounts as decimals, where the point separates rupees from paise. So ₹45.75 is 45 rupees and 75 paise. At Grade 4 children convert between rupees-and-paise and decimal form, add and subtract amounts, multiply a price by a quantity, and solve bill and change problems.

faq.q: Why do paise always need two digits after the point?
faq.a: Because one rupee is 100 paise, the paise part behaves like hundredths. Two digits keep the value clear: 5 paise is ₹0.05, while ₹0.5 would mean 50 paise. Missing that zero is the most common mistake at this age.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to add or subtract money amounts?
faq.a: Line up the decimal points one under the other before you add or subtract. That puts rupees above rupees and paise above paise automatically. If an amount has no paise, write it with .00 so both numbers have the same length.

faq.q: How do you multiply a price like ₹4.50 by a quantity?
faq.a: Ignore the point, multiply the whole numbers, then put the point back two places from the right. So 4.50 × 6 becomes 450 × 6 = 2700, which is ₹27.00. It works because you are really multiplying paise.
